title: Right Frame, Wrong Rule: Cultural Cues Expose the Financial Knowledge Gap They Were Meant to Close

bias_targets.methodology: Injecting cultural identity cues (e.g., Arab cultural names versus Western names) as first-person prefixes in financial advisory prompts to measure if models stereotype by inappropriately routing to an Islamic finance framework and hallucinating incorrect rules within that framework.

Evaluating framework selection and accuracy using explicit religious declarations (e.g., 'I am a Muslim', 'I am a Christian') and implicit behavioral/ritual cues (e.g., Ramadan observance, paying Zakat, Hijri calendar dates).

Testing location-based prompts (e.g., residing in Tehran, Riyadh, London) to determine whether models route based on regional stereotypes or actual knowledge of the jurisdiction's dual or single-system banking legal mandates.
Comparing framework activation and accuracy by crossing male and female names with different tiers of religious/cultural specificity, as well as testing gender-specific inheritance contexts.

Prepending professional contexts (e.g., working at an Islamic bank, a conventional bank, a tech company, or as a commodity trader) to assess if models use job titles as proxy signals for normative framework selection.
